content.title: Dancing with a Protocol
content.excerpt: An opinion piece by Michal Zmora and Shir Elias on the advantages and disadvantages of working by protocol in trauma therapy, and on flexibility and pacing in therapeutic work.
content.body:
At Metiv, we have been researching, teaching, supervising and treating trauma for 30 years. Much effort has gone into learning and researching treatment, and still we are far from fully understanding the best possible care for people living with post-traumatic stress. Our experience shows that going back to past experiences, associations and therapeutic conversation often fail to bring sufficient improvement and relief, or a reduction in post-traumatic symptoms.

As trauma therapists, we encounter the intense nature and powerful impact of trauma. This intensity stems from, and is suited to, the survival system, which switches on quickly and automatically in the face of danger and mobilizes great forces to keep a person alive. After the traumatic event, if these forces persist, they turn from an advantage into a disadvantage, creating helplessness and painful feelings of being stuck and of despair, in both the client and the therapist. As a result, we see a relatively common phenomenon of dropping out of therapy, and sometimes even a deepening of the damage caused by the trauma. Avoiding touching the trauma, difficulty coming to therapy and being present in it, as well as excessive flooding (or swings between these states), are very typical of these conditions and make up a significant part of the challenge of treatment.

In the face of flooding and threat, loneliness and the sense of being stuck, organizing around a protocol allows for planned, orderly work, graded yet committed, which protects the therapy from avoidance on the one hand and from flooding on the other. Because the work is structured and clear, it gives both the client and the therapist a sense of control, reduces avoidance and lowers the sense of threat.

Trauma survivors usually suffer from many difficulties in managing their lives, and addressing these difficulties often takes up all the attention and therapeutic work. Conscious and unconscious motivations trigger avoidance of the flooding that touching the trauma might bring on, so therapy can go on for a long time without any direct attention to the trauma underlying the symptoms. A trauma-focused protocol can help keep the work focused on the trauma.

Furthermore, trauma brings about such significant changes that it sometimes looks like a personality disorder of some kind (narcissistic, borderline, even schizophrenia). In these situations, therapy may focus on the behavior rather than on the traumatic events that caused it. Looking through the lens of trauma and its diagnosis can be helpful in these situations.

**At the same time, working with a protocol also has disadvantages, which therapists who use protocols should be aware of, steering the therapy so as to maximize the advantages and minimize the disadvantages.**

Here are some of the disadvantages of working strictly by protocol:

  * **"I did it to him"**

We often hear therapists say, "I did psychoeducation with him, I did regulation with him...". Such expressions can suggest that protocols can be applied to a person as an object, whereas in trauma therapy one of the important things is to bring the person back from being an object of the trauma to being a subject who influences and directs their own life.

  * **"An invisible illness"**

Trauma resembles "invisible illnesses," in which a person experiences a lack of understanding and recognition from those around them. Often the fight for recognition and the anger over its absence (which therapists sometimes tend to read as resistance to therapy, or as being stuck in "victimhood") become obstacles to progress in structured protocol work that combines measurement and assessment of symptoms.

  * **"Post-traumatic being"**

Using protocols can lead to seeing the client as "a collection of symptoms" and missing significant layers of the experience of "being post-traumatic." Issues of connection, with recognition and validation, are extremely significant in trauma therapy. The post-traumatic experience includes, for example, the experience of living in two parallel times (present and past), the experience of being torn away from human society, from innocence and from the ability to simply be, and of course familiar complex states of coping with moral injury, existential rupture and so on. All of these may get lost in work that is bound to a protocol.

Trauma-focused treatments often fail to "eliminate" the symptoms, and when the center of gravity leans almost entirely toward reducing symptoms, a sense of failure and a perceived inability to affect the person's condition may arise.

It is important to keep in mind that even in these situations, where the symptoms do not disappear, it is possible to help the person cope better with the symptoms that disrupt their life, and this too has a significant beneficial effect on the survivor's quality of life.

  * **"The pace of the work"**

Sticking too closely to a protocol can dictate a pace of work that does not match the pace of inner processes. Each person has a different nervous system, with a different history, flexibility and pace. In protocol-based therapy, the therapist often leads the treatment rather than following what is happening at the pace of the person's natural healing systems.

## Protocol and client - can they walk together?

Some therapists hold the view that when a client does not cooperate with a protocol, or is ambivalent toward it, they are probably benefiting from the secondary gains that come with their status as someone with post-traumatic stress, or are entrenched in a victim position for personality reasons.

Beyond the issue of avoidance, which is central to the response after trauma, there is also the possibility that alongside the part that wants the trauma and its impact to disappear, the client also has a part that opposes this, out of a deep, sometimes unconscious understanding that what has been done cannot be undone, and even if the client suffers less, the trauma has already been inscribed in mind and body, and has changed and affected them deeply.

Other points that deserve special attention are realization and acceptance. People who have been through trauma often experience it as "a movie," "a hallucination," something unreal. It is also common to feel that the trauma is still going on and that one is still under immediate threat. This feeling often remains even when the person knows cognitively that the trauma is over, but the sense of life's fragility has left its mark for good.

### **"What do we do? Stay flexible"**

The significant challenge in working with trauma is the ability to perform a delicate, careful and sensitive "dance": between acceptance and processing, between leading the process and quietly following it. The pace of the dance should be guided by the client's inner pace, or by the capacities of the client's nervous system, rather than by the protocol.

Protocol-based therapy can provide an organized and protective feeling, one that presents the process and the path as something one can look toward, a therapy that helps improve presence at the expense of avoidance.

Despite the efficacy of protocols as they have been researched and taught, the "planned magic" often does not happen in the clinic, and there are many possible reasons for this, as detailed in this article.

In many cases, working with protocols needs to be considered, flexible and specifically tailored to the person's way of coping, and it is always worth remembering that there are also experiences "beyond the protocol" that trauma therapy should address.

A drop in symptom measures is not the only possible outcome of trauma therapy. Sometimes there is no improvement in the measures, yet the person reports feeling better, a more meaningful life and inner calm following therapy.

We suggest using protocols as part of a broad approach to trauma therapy that takes into account the different layers of its impact. Therapists who cling to protocols may "solve" their own problem of helplessness, and even reduce symptoms, at the cost of losing the deep, intimate and close connection with the client.

Sometimes a therapist offers a client protocol-based work while taking presence and understanding for granted. Because trauma impairs presence (being a dissociative disorder that forces a person to disconnect and withdraw from different parts of reality and of the psyche in order to survive), there is a reasonable chance that we explained the protocol and the process to the survivor but they did not take it in. It is therefore advisable not to assume presence or understanding, but to check for them carefully and to avoid seeming cooperation, which ultimately undermines the person's ability to benefit from focused treatment.

Remember - beyond all the protocol-based methods, therapy succeeds in changing a condition defined psychiatrically as "post-traumatic stress disorder" in only 30-40 percent of clients. This means that for very many people treatment is not effective enough, at least by the measures commonly used today (and that is without counting those who drop out of therapy along the way).

Trauma is terrible and hard, and it stirs in us the wish to help, and in this sense the protocol-based view has importance and meaning. But given the body of knowledge we have about trauma and its consequences, it is important that we not delude ourselves, and that we stay alert and attentive to the subtle aspects of trauma, which are of enormous significance and which a protocol-based view may miss. We therefore need to keep asking questions and looking for more ways to broaden the help we offer.

**Metiv, the Psychotrauma Center in Jerusalem, works in treatment, research, supervision, training and learning in the field of post-traumatic stress. Since October 7, the center's activity has expanded, both in treating a range of populations and in research, courses and trauma treatment training programs for therapists.**
